topic_title: Top 10 Hypoallergenic Dog Breeds for Allergy Sufferers
intro: Dog allergies come from proteins in dander, saliva and urine, not from hair itself, so no breed is truly allergen-free. What a low-shedding coat does is hold loose hair and dander until it is brushed or clipped out, which keeps less of it on floors and furniture. That trade comes with grooming: most of these coats need regular brushing and professional trims. Before committing, spend several hours with the breed, ideally the actual dog, and keep the dog out of the bedroom.

picks.description: The Papillon is a small dog of 5 to 10 pounds with a fine, silky single coat and no undercoat, so it sheds lightly and never mats badly. Brushing once or twice a week is usually enough, and no professional clipping is needed, which makes it the easiest coat on this list. The trade-off is energy: Papillons are high-energy and very quick learners, so they need daily walks plus training games, and many excel at agility. They are friendly and good with children, cats and other dogs, but their fine bones mean supervision around young kids and furniture jumps. Barking is moderate and often alert-driven. It ranks last here because some hair is still shed, so it suits people with milder allergies.
picks.best_for: Active owners with mild allergies wanting a small, trainable dog
picks.quirky_fact: Papillon is French for butterfly, after the breed's large, fringed upright ears.
picks.skip_if: Your allergies are severe or you want a low-energy lap dog

picks.description: The Affenpinscher is a toy-sized terrier type of about 7 to 10 pounds with a rough, wiry coat that sheds little and needs less upkeep than the silky or curly breeds: brushing once or twice a week and a tidy-up trim every couple of months. Energy is medium; short walks and indoor play keep it content. Affens are curious, playful and affectionate with their people, and good with cats and other dogs. They can live with children, but their small size and sometimes stubborn streak suit older, calmer kids better than toddlers. Training is moderate and takes patience, especially house-training. Barking is moderate, often at unfamiliar sounds. It is a good choice for allergy-prone owners who want a small dog with a lower grooming bill.
picks.best_for: Owners with allergies wanting a small, low-grooming, comical companion
picks.quirky_fact: Affenpinscher means monkey terrier in German, a reference to the breed's expressive, monkey-like face.
picks.skip_if: You have very young children or want a dog that trains quickly

picks.description: The Miniature Schnauzer offers the same wiry, light-shedding coat as its larger cousin in an 11 to 20 pound body. Its grooming is similar: weekly brushing, regular beard cleaning and a clip or hand-strip every five to eight weeks. Energy is medium, so a couple of brisk walks and some play each day are enough, and it adapts well to apartments if exercised. Minis are easy to train, friendly, and good with children, cats and other dogs, though their terrier background shows in a keen interest in small animals outdoors. Barking is the main drawback: they are quick to alert at doorbells and passers-by, so teaching a quiet cue early matters. They usually live 12 to 15 years and stay playful well into middle age.
picks.best_for: Small homes with allergies wanting a sturdy, playful, trainable dog
picks.quirky_fact: Miniature Schnauzers were bred in Germany as farm ratters, which explains their quick reactions to small moving things.
picks.skip_if: Thin walls or close neighbors make alert barking a real problem

picks.description: The Standard Schnauzer is a medium dog of about 30 to 50 pounds with a harsh, wiry outer coat and a dense undercoat that sheds lightly. Grooming is moderate: weekly brushing, a trim of the beard and eyebrows, and either hand-stripping or clipping every few months. The beard can hold food and water, so it needs wiping after meals. Energy is medium, but this is a sharp working breed that needs a daily walk plus training or games to stay out of trouble. Schnauzers are easy to train, loyal and good with children, cats and other dogs when raised with them. They are alert watchdogs and will bark at strangers. For allergy sufferers who want a sturdier dog than the toy breeds, this is a sensible medium-size option.
picks.best_for: Active owners with allergies wanting a medium, alert, trainable dog
picks.quirky_fact: The Standard Schnauzer is the original Schnauzer; the Miniature and Giant were later bred from it.
picks.skip_if: You want a quiet dog or can't provide daily mental work

picks.description: The Shih Tzu is a calm, low-energy small dog, usually 9 to 16 pounds, with a long, flowing coat that sheds little but tangles easily. A full coat needs daily brushing, so many owners choose a short trim every six to eight weeks, plus a topknot or face trim to keep hair out of the eyes. Short walks and indoor play cover its exercise. Shih Tzus are affectionate and good with children, cats and other dogs, and they bark moderately. Training is moderate: they can be stubborn, and house-training in particular rewards consistency. The flat face makes them sensitive to heat, so summer walks belong in the cool hours and the home needs air conditioning in hot climates. Lifespan is wide, roughly 10 to 16 years.
picks.best_for: Calm homes with allergies wanting a relaxed, affectionate lap dog
picks.quirky_fact: The name Shih Tzu translates roughly as little lion, a nod to the breed's history in the Chinese imperial court.
picks.skip_if: You live somewhere hot without air conditioning or want a quick learner

picks.description: The Bichon Frise, about 12 to 18 pounds, has a curly outer coat over a soft undercoat, and shed hair stays trapped in it rather than landing on furniture. That is helpful for allergies but means mats form quickly: brush several times a week and book a professional trim every four to six weeks. Bichons have medium energy, met with daily walks and play, and they are easy to train with short, upbeat sessions, though house-training can take patience. They are playful and good with children, cats and other dogs, and bark at a moderate level. White coats show tear and mouth staining, so a quick daily face wipe helps. Bichons are sociable and do best with someone home for much of the day.
picks.best_for: Families with allergies wanting a playful, people-loving small dog
picks.quirky_fact: Bichons often do a burst of fast laps around the room, which owners call the Bichon blitz.
picks.skip_if: You can't commit to frequent brushing or the dog would often be alone

picks.description: The Havanese weighs about 7 to 13 pounds and has a soft, long coat that sheds little, with loose hair caught in the coat until it is brushed out. That means brushing several times a week, or a short trim every six to eight weeks if you don't want to keep it long. Energy is medium: a couple of walks and some indoor play satisfy it, and it is sturdy enough for gentle play with children. Havanese are easy to train, cheerful and good with kids, cats and other dogs. They bark to announce visitors but are not usually nuisance barkers. The main drawback is that they bond closely and dislike being left alone, so households that are out all day should look at a more independent breed or plan for midday company.
picks.best_for: Households with allergies wanting a sturdy, cheerful small dog
picks.quirky_fact: The Havanese is the national dog of Cuba and was developed from small companion dogs brought there by Spanish settlers.
picks.skip_if: Everyone is out all day, since Havanese struggle when left alone for long

picks.description: The Maltese is a toy breed under 7 pounds with a single-layer coat of long, silky white hair and no woolly undercoat, which is why it sheds very little. Its small size also means less total coat and dander in the house than a larger low-shedding dog. The trade-off is grooming: a full-length coat needs daily brushing, so most pet owners keep a short puppy clip trimmed every few weeks, and the face needs regular wiping to limit tear stains. Energy is low, so short walks and indoor play are enough. Maltese are gentle, easy to train and good with children, cats and other dogs, though their small frame needs careful handling around toddlers. They can bark at noises and dislike long stretches alone.
picks.best_for: Apartment dwellers with allergies wanting a calm, tiny lap dog
picks.quirky_fact: The Maltese has been kept as a companion dog in the Mediterranean for well over two thousand years.
picks.skip_if: You have rough toddlers or the dog would be alone for long workdays

picks.description: The Lagotto Romagnolo is a medium-sized Italian water dog, roughly 24 to 35 pounds, with a dense, woolly coat of curls that sheds very little. The coat needs regular attention: brushing through to the skin every week or two to prevent mats, plus a full trim a few times a year. Lagottos have medium energy, so a long daily walk plus a sniffing game or training session keeps them settled. They are affectionate, good with children, cats and other dogs, and live 14 to 16 years. Training is moderate rather than easy; they are clever but follow their noses and can dig in the yard if bored. Barking is moderate. For an allergy-prone family that wants something between a toy breed and a large Poodle, it is a good middle size.
picks.best_for: Families wanting a medium, low-shedding dog with moderate energy
picks.quirky_fact: The Lagotto is the classic truffle-hunting dog of Italy, prized for its nose rather than for retrieving game.
picks.skip_if: You want a dog that never needs trimming or dislike holes dug in the garden

picks.description: The Standard Poodle is the most common recommendation for allergy-prone households because its tight, curly coat catches loose hair and dander instead of dropping it on the sofa. That coat keeps growing, so plan on brushing several times a week and a professional clip every four to eight weeks. This is a large, athletic dog, usually 40 to 70 pounds, and it needs an hour or more of exercise daily, such as brisk walks, fetch or swimming. Poodles are among the easiest breeds to train and are good with children, cats and other dogs. Barking is moderate, often as an alert. If you want the same coat in a smaller package, the Miniature and Toy Poodle share it, but this pick is about the standard size and its steadier temperament.
picks.best_for: Active allergy sufferers wanting a large, trainable, low-shedding family dog
picks.quirky_fact: The traditional poodle show clip began as a working cut that kept joints and chest warm while lightening the coat for retrieving in water.
picks.skip_if: You can't give an hour of daily exercise or budget for regular professional grooming

faqs.question: Is any dog breed truly hypoallergenic?
faqs.answer: No. The proteins that trigger dog allergies are in skin flakes, saliva and urine, and every dog produces them. Low-shedding breeds can still help because their coats hold loose hair and dander until grooming removes it, so less of it ends up around the house. Individual dogs vary too, which is why meeting the specific dog before you commit matters more than the breed label.

faqs.question: Which low-shedding dog is best for a small home?
faqs.answer: The Maltese, Havanese, Bichon Frise and Shih Tzu are the smaller low-shedding options on this list, and all get along with children, cats and other dogs. The Maltese and Shih Tzu have the lowest energy, so short walks and indoor play cover their exercise. All four need frequent brushing or a short trim to keep their coats from matting.

faqs.question: How much grooming do low-shedding dogs need?
faqs.answer: More than most people expect. Poodles, Lagottos, Maltese, Havanese, Bichons and Shih Tzus have coats that keep growing, so they need brushing several times a week and a professional trim roughly every four to eight weeks. The wire-coated Schnauzers and Affenpinscher need less brushing but benefit from hand-stripping or clipping a few times a year. Skipping grooming leads to mats and trapped dander.

faqs.question: How can I reduce dog allergens at home?
faqs.answer: Keep the dog out of the bedroom, run a HEPA air purifier in the main living area, vacuum with a HEPA-filter vacuum a few times a week, and wash the dog's bedding weekly. Have someone without allergies do the brushing outdoors if possible. Bathing helps for a few days, but too-frequent baths dry the skin, so ask your vet about a sensible schedule.

faqs.question: Should I see a doctor before getting a dog with allergies?
faqs.answer: It is a sensible step, especially if you have asthma or strong reactions. An allergist can confirm whether dogs are the trigger and discuss treatment options. Then spend real time around the breed you are considering, ideally visiting the same dog more than once, before you bring one home, since rehoming a dog later is hard on everyone.

seo_title: Hypoallergenic Dog Breeds for Allergies (2026 Guide)
answer: The Standard Poodle, Lagotto Romagnolo and Maltese are the strongest low-shedding picks here for people with dog allergies. No breed is allergen-free, so the deciding factor is a coat that holds loose hair and dander instead of dropping it, plus your own reaction after time with the dog.
method: We filtered a 150-breed dataset for breeds rated low for shedding, then ordered them by coat type, grooming needs, temperament with kids and other pets, and energy, putting the most widely recommended low-shedding coats first.
